name: Afagddu

attributes.attribute: also spelled Yfagdddu, meaning utter darkness

sources: MacCulloch, J. A. The Religion of the Ancient Celts. London: Constable, 1911, 116.
Straffon, Cheryl. The Earth Goddess: Celtic and Pagan Legacy of the Landscape. London: Blandford, 1997, 43.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Afagddu, also spelled Yfagdddu, was a boy of great plainness in Welsh myth. His name means utter darkness. People also knew him as Morfran, the sea crow. That was his second name. His mother, the hag-goddess Ceridwen, feared that no woman would take him. She brewed herbs in her cauldron, so that the power of verse might win him a wife. The servant Gwion drank the brew too early. He drank away its magic and rose as the great poet Taliesin. After that the tale tells nothing more of Afagddu. It is uncertain whether the cauldron bore Morfran as an ugly brother or as a second name.

okr.objective: Record the myth of Afagddu and the stolen magic.
key_results: Explain the name and the mother.
Tell how Gwion rose as Taliesin.
Give the alternative spellings and the name Morfran.
